phase.label: The Ferrara camerino for Alfonso d’Este, 1518–23

source.label: Wikipedia: “one of a cycle of paintings on mythological subjects produced for Alfonso I d'Este, Duke of Ferrara”
Wikipedia: the blue sky uses “the expensive ultramarine pigment”

highlight.text: The composition is divided diagonally into two triangles, one of blue sky, using the expensive ultramarine pigment, and still but for the two lovers caught in movement, the other a riot of movement and predominantly green/brown in colour.

source.label: Wikipedia: “a very early treatment of subjects from classical mythology on a heroic scale in painting”
Wikipedia: “Along with Giorgione, he is considered a founder of the Venetian school of Italian Renaissance painting”

work.text: In the Bacchus and Ariadne Titian's genius flames up with an intensity of passion such as will hardly again be seen to illuminate it in an imaginative subject of this class.
the series being completed a little later on by that crown and climax of the whole set, the Bacchus and Ariadne of the National Gallery.

moment.text: An advance payment was given to Raphael, who originally held the commission for the subject of a Triumph of Bacchus. At the time of Raphael's death in 1520, only a preliminary drawing was completed. The commission was then handed to Titian.
The series was a very early treatment of subjects from classical mythology on a heroic scale in painting, rather than in small decorative pieces, and very influential on later works.

matters.text: Falling in love with Ariadne on first sight, he leaps from his chariot, drawn by two cheetahs, towards her. Ariadne had been abandoned on the Greek island of Naxos by Theseus, whose ship is shown in the distance.

source.author: National Gallery, London
source.title: Bacchus and Ariadne (collection description, as quoted in Wikipedia’s “Bacchus and Ariadne”)

matters.text: the more I thought over it the more I became convinced that the greatness of art amongst the ancients was due to the assistance they received from great princes content to leave to the painters the credit and renown derived from their own ingenuity in bespeaking pictures.

source.author: Titian
source.title: Letter to Duke Alfonso d’Este of Ferrara, 1 April 1518 (trans. J. A. Crowe and G. B. Cavalcaselle, Titian: His Life and Times, 1877)

matters.lead: Titian to his Ferrara patron, acknowledging the duke’s instructions for another picture for the same room, 1518:

matters.text: And, in truth, gifts have great potency with those who labour for the love of art, when they are uplifted by the liberality of Princes.

source.author: Giorgio Vasari
source.title: Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors and Architects, Vol. 9 (Life of Tiziano da Cadore)
source.publisher: Translated by Gaston du C. de Vere (Project Gutenberg)
